Remedies for Breach of Contract 
199
(2016 version)
Art. 1221.—​A creditor of an obligation may, having given notice to perform, seek 
performance in kind unless performance is impossible or if there is a manifest dis­
proportion between its cost to the debtor and its interest for the creditor.
(2018 version)
Art. 1221.—​A creditor of an obligation may, having given notice to perform, 
seek performance in kind unless performance is impossible or if there is a mani­
fest disproportion between its cost to the debtor acting in good faith and its 
interest for the creditor.
Art. 1341.—​A creditor has the right to performance of the obligation; he may 
compel the debtor to perform under the conditions provided by legislation.
Nearly all obligations are specifically enforceable in French law. An injured party 
can enforce both monetary and non-​monetary obligations in most circum­
stances.25 It is a very effective remedy, to a large extent because French courts are 
prepared to deploy significant means in order to give effect to the contract.
(a)  The formal recognition of specific enforcement as a remedy
New articles 1217 and 1221 both provide that, upon breach, the injured party can 
seek specific enforcement of the contract. This has been a central remedy in French 
law for many years and was widely available before the reforms, despite an ap­
parent conflict in the 1804 Civil Code on the point. Specifically, the stipulation in 
paragraph 2 of old article 1184 that the injured party could compel the defaulting 
party to perform where performance was still possible26 appeared at odds with the 
emphasis on damages to the exclusion of other remedies in old article 1142, which 
stated that ‘every obligation to do or not to do gives rise to liability in damages in 
cases of non-​performance by the promisor’. In practice, however, the apparent pre­
cedence given to damages was always construed restrictively. The courts consist­
ently found that damages did not have to be the main or only remedy. Article 1142 
was instead interpreted narrowly, as being confined to obligations of a personal 
character which could not be specifically enforced.27 This approach is adopted in 
the new Civil Code, confirming specific enforcement as a broadly available and 
central remedy in France, which is an article of faith amongst French lawyers.28
	
25	 The enforcement of monetary obligations is dealt with separately at article 1341 of the Civil Code 
but this merely affirms what article 1221 provides in respect of non-​monetary obligations.
	
26	 See also article 1228 of the 1804 Civil Code and article 1 of law 9 July 1991 on the reform of 
civil enforcement procedures (loi no 91-​650 du 9 juillet 1991 portant réforme des procédures civiles 
d’exécution).
	
27	 Civ 20 Jan 1953, JCP 1953.II.7677, note P Esmein.
	
28	 Chantepie and Latina (n 13) [636]; Y-​M Laithier, ‘Exécution Forcée en Nature’ in J Cartwright and 
S Whittaker (eds), The Code Napoléon Rewritten: French Contract Law after the 2016 Reforms (Hart 
Publishing: Oxford, 2017) 281.
